items.stem: Which set contains −4 but not 0.5?
items.answer: ℤ
items.markingKey: B. ℤ is the integers: −4 is an integer but 0.5 is not.

items.stem: Explain the difference between irrational numbers and rational numbers.
items.answer: Rationals can be written as a/b with integers (terminating or recurring decimals); irrationals cannot (non-terminating, non-recurring decimals).
items.markingKey: Rationals can be written as a/b with integers (terminating or recurring decimals); irrationals cannot (non-terminating, non-recurring decimals). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why every recurring decimal is a rational number.
items.answer: A recurring decimal can be turned into a fraction (e.g. multiply by a power of 10 and subtract), so it can be written as a/b with integers a and b. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A recurring decimal can be turned into a fraction (e.g. multiply by a power of 10 and subtract), so it can be written as a/b with integers a and b. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Solve |4x − 3| = 4.
For each number, state the smallest of the sets ℕ, ℤ, ℚ or "irrational" that contains it: 9/4, √18, √9, 3π, −8, 0.
items.answer: 9/4: ℚ; √18: irrational; √9: ℕ; 3π: irrational; −8: ℤ; 0: ℤ
items.markingKey: 9/4: ℚ; √18: irrational; √9: ℕ; 3π: irrational; −8: ℤ; 0: ℤ. A1 for every two correct; simplify roots such as √(perfect square) first (criterion C: correct set symbols).

items.stem: Food regulations in Malaysia say a fridge must stay between 2 °C and 7 °C inclusive. (a) Write the safe temperatures T in interval notation. (b) Write the condition as a single absolute-value inequality and explain how you found its numbers. (c) A sensor reads 0 °C. Use your inequality to decide whether this is safe.
items.answer: (a) [2, 7] (b) centre 4.5 °C, half-width 2.5 °C: |T − 4.5| ≤ 2.5 (c) |0 − 4.5| = 4.5 > 2.5, so 0 °C is outside the safe range
items.markingKey: (a) [2, 7] (b) centre 4.5 °C, half-width 2.5 °C: |T − 4.5| ≤ 2.5 (c) |0 − 4.5| = 4.5 > 2.5, so 0 °C is outside the safe range. Absolute-value statement (A1); interval notation (A1 C1); values tested correctly (M1 A1); reasoning in context (D: R1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "real numbers"?
options: Using the fact that if a^m = a^n (a > 0, a ≠ 1) then m = n
The set ℝ of all rational and irrational numbers; every point on the number line
The distance of a number from zero on the number line, written |x|; it is never negative
Rewriting a fraction so that no surd remains in its denominator, by multiplying top and bottom by a suitable surd or conjugate
items.answer: The set ℝ of all rational and irrational numbers; every point on the number line
items.markingKey: B. "real numbers" is the set ℝ of all rational and irrational numbers; every point on the number line.

items.stem: Briefly explain why |a − b| gives the distance between a and b on the number line.
items.answer: Subtracting gives the signed gap between the numbers; taking the absolute value removes the sign, so the result is the length of the gap whichever number is larger.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Subtracting gives the signed gap between the numbers; taking the absolute value removes the sign, so the result is the length of the gap whichever number is larger. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: It contains every real number strictly between 1 and 4, for example 1.5 and π.

items.stem: Hana solves |x − 2| > 2 and writes 0 > x > 4. Explain why this is wrong and give the correct solution.
items.answer: No number is both less than 0 and greater than 4; the solution is two separate pieces: x < 0 or x > 4.
items.markingKey: Contradiction identified (R1); correct union stated (A1).

items.stem: Investigate the product (√n + 1)(√n − 1). (a) Evaluate it for n = 10, 13, 7. (b) Describe the pattern. (c) Prove your conjecture algebraically. (d) Use it to write down (√56 + 1)(√56 − 1).

items.markingKey: (a) (√10 + 1)(√10 − 1) = 9; (√13 + 1)(√13 − 1) = 12; (√7 + 1)(√7 − 1) = 6 (b) the result is always one less than the number under the root (c) (√n + 1)(√n − 1) = n − √n + √n − 1 = n − 1 (d) 55. items.stem: Explain why a^(1/2) = √a, using the laws of exponents.
items.answer: (a^(1/2))² = a^(1/2 × 2) = a¹ = a, so a^(1/2) is the positive number whose square is a, which is √a.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: (a^(1/2))² = a^(1/2 × 2) = a¹ = a, so a^(1/2) is the positive number whose square is a, which is √a. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a^(1/n) and a/n.

items.stem: Briefly explain why multiplying by the conjugate removes the surd from a denominator such as 3 + √2.
items.answer: (3 + √2)(3 − √2) = 9 − 2 = 7: the cross terms cancel and √2 × √2 is rational, so the denominator becomes rational.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: (3 + √2)(3 − √2) = 9 − 2 = 7: the cross terms cancel and √2 × √2 is rational, so the denominator becomes rational. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why 2^x = −8 has no real solution.
items.answer: 2^x is positive for every real x, so it can never equal a negative number.

items.answer: (a) N = 100 × 2^(t/20) (b) 800 bacteria (c) 1,600 = 100 × 2⁴ so t/20 = 4, t = 80 minutes (d) real growth slows when food or space runs out
items.markingKey: (a) N = 100 × 2^(t/20) (b) 800 bacteria (c) 1,600 = 100 × 2⁴ so t/20 = 4, t = 80 minutes (d) real growth slows when food or space runs out. Model or common base set up (M1); exponents equated and solved (A1 A1); pattern generalised (B: R1); interpretation in context (D: R1).

items.stem: Solve 2^x = 64.
Explain why the equation 27^x = −9 has no real solution, while 27^x = 1/9 does.
items.answer: 27^x > 0 for every real x, so it cannot be negative; 1/9 = 3^(−2) is positive, giving x = −2/3.
items.markingKey: Positivity of exponentials (R1); second equation solved (A1).

items.stem: Explain why the equation 27^x = −81 has no real solution, while 27^x = 1/81 does.
items.answer: 27^x > 0 for every real x, so it cannot be negative; 1/81 = 3^(−4) is positive, giving x = −4/3.

items.stem: A charity in Oslo starts a message chain: in round 1 one person sends it to 2 people, and in every later round each new receiver sends it to 2 more. (a) Write the number of new receivers in rounds 1, 2 and 3. (b) Write an expression for round n. (c) Without a calculator, find the round in which 64 new people receive it. (d) Find the total number of receivers in the first 6 rounds.
items.markingKey: (a) 2, 4, 8 (b) 2^n (c) 2^n = 64 = 2⁶, so n = 6 rounds (d) total = 2(2⁶ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 126. Model or common base set up (M1); exponents equated and solved (A1 A1); pattern generalised (B: R1); interpretation in context (D: R1).

items.stem: "If 2^x = 2^5 × 2^3, then x = 15." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Multiplying powers adds exponents: 2^5 × 2^3 = 2^8, so x = 8.
items.markingKey: Multiplying powers adds exponents: 2^5 × 2^3 = 2^8, so x = 8. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A rectangular frame measures 72 cm by 13 cm, each to the nearest cm. Find the lower and upper bounds of its perimeter.
items.answer: lower 168 cm, upper 172 cm
items.markingKey: Bounds ±0.5 on each side (M1); LB (A1); UB (A1).

items.stem: "The interval (1, 4) contains the numbers 2 and 3 only." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It contains every real number strictly between 1 and 4, for example 1.5 and π.
items.markingKey: It contains every real number strictly between 1 and 4, for example 1.5 and π. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "A length of 12 cm to the nearest cm has upper bound 12.4 cm." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The upper bound is 12.5 cm (the boundary at which it would round up).
items.markingKey: The upper bound is 12.5 cm (the boundary at which it would round up). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A designer in Dubai makes square tiles of area 96 cm². (a) Find the side length in simplest surd form. (b) Find the perimeter in simplest surd form. (c) Find the length of the diagonal in simplest surd form. (d) Give the diagonal to 3 significant figures and explain why the exact form is useful.
items.answer: (a) √96 = 4√6 cm (b) 16√6 cm (c) diagonal = 4√6 × √2 = 8√3 cm (d) about 13.9 cm; exact form avoids rounding errors in later steps
items.markingKey: (a) √96 = 4√6 cm (b) 16√6 cm (c) diagonal = 4√6 × √2 = 8√3 cm (d) about 13.9 cm; exact form avoids rounding errors in later steps. Surds simplified exactly (A1 A1); method/proof communicated (B/C: M1 R1); answer in context with sensible accuracy (D: A1).

items.stem: For international records, a 50 m pool in Melbourne must have lanes whose length L metres is within 0.01 m of 50 m. (a) Write the condition with absolute value. (b) Write it in interval notation. (c) Lanes were measured as 50.02, 50.03, 50.04 m. Which lanes are outside the tolerance? (d) Suggest why such a strict tolerance is needed.
items.answer: (a) |L − 50| ≤ 0.01 (b) [49.99, 50.01] (c) outside: 50.02, 50.03, 50.04 (d) records need fair, comparable distances
items.markingKey: (a) |L − 50| ≤ 0.01 (b) [49.99, 50.01] (c) outside: 50.02, 50.03, 50.04 (d) records need fair, comparable distances. Absolute-value statement (A1); interval notation (A1 C1); values tested correctly (M1 A1); reasoning in context (D: R1).

items.stem: A knockout tennis tournament in Melbourne halves the number of players each round until one champion is left. (a) Explain why the number of players should be a power of 2. (b) With 16 players, find the number of rounds by solving an exponential equation. (c) Find the total number of matches. (d) Write a formula for the number of matches with 2^n players.
items.answer: (a) 2^n players allow n rounds (b) 16 = 2⁴, so 4 rounds (c) 15 matches (one player is knocked out per match) (d) 2^n − 1
items.markingKey: (a) 2^n players allow n rounds (b) 16 = 2⁴, so 4 rounds (c) 15 matches (one player is knocked out per match) (d) 2^n − 1. Model or common base set up (M1); exponents equated and solved (A1 A1); pattern generalised (B: R1); interpretation in context (D: R1).

items.stem: At an athletics meeting in Lima, a runner covers 400 m (to the nearest metre) in 17.3 s (to the nearest 0.1 s). (a) Write the bounds of the distance and the time. (b) Find the average speed using the recorded values, to 4 s.f. (c) Find the lower and upper bounds of the speed to 4 s.f. (d) Explain which bounds you used for the upper bound of speed.
items.answer: (a) d in [399.5, 400.5), t in [17.25, 17.35) (b) 23.12 m/s (c) lower 23.03 m/s, upper 23.22 m/s (d) max distance ÷ min time gives the largest speed
items.markingKey: (a) d in [399.5, 400.5), t in [17.25, 17.35) (b) 23.12 m/s (c) lower 23.03 m/s, upper 23.22 m/s (d) max distance ÷ min time gives the largest speed. Percentage error or bounds formula used correctly (M1 A1 A1); comparison or check carried out (D: R1); conclusion communicated with suitable accuracy (C1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "interval notation".
items.answer: A way of writing a set of real numbers between two endpoints, using [ ] for included endpoints and ( ) for excluded ones, e.g. (−2, 5]
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a way of writing a set of real numbers between two endpoints, using [ ] for included endpoints and ( ) for excluded ones, e.g. (−2, 5]. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Write 8^x as a power of 2.
Sana says the percentage error of estimating 33 as 36 is |36 − 33| ÷ 36 × 100 = 8.33%. Explain the mistake and correct it.
items.answer: Divide by the exact value 33, not the estimate: 9.09%.
items.markingKey: Mistake identified (R1); correct value (A1).

items.stem: Explain why a^0 = 1 for any non-zero a.
items.answer: aⁿ ÷ aⁿ = 1, but by the division law it is also a^(n − n) = a⁰, so a⁰ = 1.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: aⁿ ÷ aⁿ = 1, but by the division law it is also a^(n − n) = a⁰, so a⁰ = 1. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between rational numbers and irrational numbers.
items.answer: Rationals can be written as a/b with integers (terminating or recurring decimals); irrationals cannot (non-terminating, non-recurring decimals).
items.markingKey: Rationals can be written as a/b with integers (terminating or recurring decimals); irrationals cannot (non-terminating, non-recurring decimals). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Chloé solves 3^x + 3^x = 3² by writing 3^(2x) = 3². Explain the error and solve the equation correctly.
items.answer: 3^x + 3^x = 2 × 3^x, not 3^(2x) (adding does not add exponents). So 2 × 3^x = 3^2, 3^x = 3^2/2, which needs logarithms: x = 1.37.
items.markingKey: Error explained (R1); correct solution (A1).

items.stem: Explain why the absolute value is used in the percentage-error formula.
items.answer: The error is a size; overestimates and underestimates of the same amount should give the same positive percentage.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The error is a size; overestimates and underestimates of the same amount should give the same positive percentage. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why 9^(3/2) can be worked out as (√9)³ and evaluate it.
items.answer: 9^(3/2) = (9^(1/2))³ by the power law; √9 = 3, so the value is 3³ = 27.
items.markingKey: Power law justification (R1); value (A1).

items.stem: For each number, state the smallest of the sets ℕ, ℤ, ℚ or "irrational" that contains it: 15, π, −1, 0, 0.777… (recurring).
items.answer: 15: ℕ; π: irrational; −1: ℤ; 0: ℤ; 0.777… (recurring): ℚ
items.markingKey: 15: ℕ; π: irrational; −1: ℤ; 0: ℤ; 0.777… (recurring): ℚ. A1 for every two correct; simplify roots such as √(perfect square) first (criterion C: correct set symbols).

A rectangular garden plot in Accra measures 4√3 m by 2√7 m. (a) Find its exact area in simplest form. (b) Find its exact perimeter. (c) Use Pythagoras' theorem to find the exact length of the diagonal. (d) Give the diagonal to 3 significant figures.
items.answer: (a) area = 4√3 × 2√7 = 8√21 m² (b) perimeter = 8√3 + 4√7 m (c) diagonal = √(48 + 28) = 2√19 m (d) about 8.72 m
items.markingKey: (a) area = 4√3 × 2√7 = 8√21 m² (b) perimeter = 8√3 + 4√7 m (c) diagonal = √(48 + 28) = 2√19 m (d) about 8.72 m. Surds simplified exactly (A1 A1); method/proof communicated (B/C: M1 R1); answer in context with sensible accuracy (D: A1).

items.stem: An airline in Toronto calls a flight "on time" if its journey time t minutes is within 15 minutes of the scheduled 165 minutes. (a) Write this as an absolute-value inequality. (b) Write it in interval notation. (c) Four flights took 185, 149, 170, 174 minutes. Which were on time, and what fraction is this? (d) Comment on the effect of changing the tolerance.
items.answer: (a) |t − 165| ≤ 15 (b) [150, 180] (c) on time: 170, 174; proportion 1/2 (d) e.g. a tighter tolerance is fairer to passengers but harder for the airline to meet
items.markingKey: (a) |t − 165| ≤ 15 (b) [150, 180] (c) on time: 170, 174; proportion 1/2 (d) e.g. a tighter tolerance is fairer to passengers but harder for the airline to meet. items.stem: A lab in Cape Town grows a culture that starts with 400 bacteria and doubles every 30 minutes. (a) Write a formula for the number N after t minutes. (b) Find N after 90 minutes. (c) Without a calculator, find when N = 6,400. (d) Explain one reason the model may fail for large t.
items.answer: (a) N = 400 × 2^(t/30) (b) 3,200 bacteria (c) 6,400 = 400 × 2⁴ so t/30 = 4, t = 120 minutes (d) real growth slows when food or space runs out
items.markingKey: (a) N = 400 × 2^(t/30) (b) 3,200 bacteria (c) 6,400 = 400 × 2⁴ so t/30 = 4, t = 120 minutes (d) real growth slows when food or space runs out. Model or common base set up (M1); exponents equated and solved (A1 A1); pattern generalised (B: R1); interpretation in context (D: R1).

items.stem: The ticket scanners at a festival in Oslo recorded 20,355 people. Estimates were: Rafael 18,000, Noah 23,000, the police 23,000. (a) Find each percentage error to 2 d.p. (b) Who was most accurate? (c) Round the true figure to the nearest thousand and give the bounds that rounded value represents. (d) Suggest a method that would give a better estimate.
items.answer: (a) Rafael: 11.57%; Noah: 12.99%; the police: 12.99% (b) Rafael (c) 20,355 people to the nearest 1000 is 20,000; bounds 19,500 ≤ n < 20,500 (d) e.g. counting in a sample area and scaling up
